You design Thai language lesson scenarios. Given vocabulary words, create a vivid realistic scene where two Thai adult friends (not family members) naturally use these words. Characters A and B are friends or acquaintances — never parent/child, never siblings.

Vocabulary: รถเมล์=bus, ยาว=long, ครั้ง=time(s), occasion, คุ้ม=to be worthwhile, ทางเข้า=entrance, ควร=should, กังวล=to worry, รีบ=hurry, หวัง=hope, คู่=pair/couple, ชิ้น=piece/classifier, ไฟ=light/electricity, ต้องการ=want, need (formal), สามารถ=be able to (formal), เล่า=tell

Plan a language lesson conversation. LESSON THEME (broad — NOT a place every scene must happen in): Somchai and Nida are discussing their travel plans. Somchai explains that the bus route is very long, but Nida reassures him it's worthwhile for the sights they'll see. They also confirm the entrance location, and Somchai expresses his hope that the lights will be on when they arrive.
Characters: A = Somchai (a curious traveler) · B = Nida (an experienced traveler)
Group these target words into 2–7 MINI-SCENES (e.g. at the stall → paying → planning the trip). Each mini-scene gets a short purpose AND its OWN localPremise (where A and B are and what is happening in THIS scene), location and immediateGoal — a travel scene is about travel even if the lesson began at a food stall. Put each word where its NORMAL meaning fits best. Use every id exactly once. Prefer several coherent mini-scenes over one forced conversation.
CLUSTER BY MEANING: words of the same semantic domain belong in the SAME mini-scene — e.g. food words (meat, garlic, onion, lime, snacks) together; shopping/payment words (promotion, discount, card, credit card, transfer) together; home words (bedroom, kitchen, shower) together; big numbers (ten thousand, hundred thousand, million) together with prices; plans/schedule words (tired, probably, Thursday, wake up) together. Mini-scenes may have very different sizes (2 words or 10 words is fine) — never split a domain just to balance the sizes. The domain hint after each word is a suggestion.

DIALOGUE RULE: These are conversation pairs. Prompts describe what a character says in third person ("He says he likes...", "She asks if...") but the Thai sentence naturally uses first person ("ผม/ฉัน = I"). This is CORRECT and NEVER a mismatch.

PERSPECTIVE RULE (apply BEFORE comparing): the prompt narrates the SPEAKER in the third person; the Thai and English are the speaker's own words. Speaker A is a man: in A's prompt "he/him/his" = "I/me/my" (ผม) and "she/her" = "you" (คุณ, the listener). Speaker B is a woman: in B's prompt "she/her" = "I/me/my" (ฉัน) and "he/him" = "you" (คุณ). THAI LEXICAL FACTS: จ่าย (pay) is ordinary spoken Thai, never "too formal". 10,000 is หนึ่งหมื่น / หมื่น (สิบพัน is not idiomatic). พอดี means "just right / fits / exactly enough" (and พอดี… at the start = "it so happens"); English "just right" does NOT require เพิ่ง (เพิ่ง = "just" in time: has just happened). เจอ + a person = "meet / see"; เจอ + a thing = "find". พี่ can ADDRESS the listener ("you", someone a little older) or mean "older sibling" — judge which by context; either is correct Thai. หน่อย softens a request or asks for "a bit more" (ช่วยหน่อย, เร็วหน่อย); it does not attach to a descriptive adjective to mean "quite".
